CANONICAL WALK-ROW PROMPT — one image per direction, landscape 1536x1024.
Fill {CHARACTER} from the game's art-style.json (including its lockedDetails),
and keep exactly ONE of the three {VIEW} blocks below. Do not ask for a 3x3
grid: square canvases clip the bottom row and tall ones drop a column. See
CHARACTER_SHEETS.md for why each sentence here is present.

---8<--- PROMPT STARTS ---8<---

A 16-bit SNES-style PIXEL ART sprite row on a SOLID FLAT PURE WHITE background (#FFFFFF, completely uniform). Exactly THREE sprites side by side in the middle of the image, evenly spaced, with a wide empty white margin on all four sides and a clear white gap between them — nothing touching, overlapping, or cut off by any edge. All three are the SAME character at the SAME size and the SAME pixel scale.

THE CHARACTER, drawn identically in all three frames: {CHARACTER}

{VIEW}

ART STYLE: chunky flat cartoon pixel art, big simple shapes, flat solid colours, a thick black outline, no anti-aliasing, no gradients, no dithering, no texture inside a colour block. Draw NO GROUND — no floor line, no bar or plinth under the feet, no platform, no shadow; the character floats on empty white and the game draws its own floor. Nothing else in the image: no grid lines, no boxes, no frames, no labels, no text, no numbers. FINAL CHECK, THE BACKGROUND: every pixel that is not one of the three sprites is PURE WHITE #FFFFFF. No backdrop, no vignette, no dark or coloured surround, no gradient, no scene, no border, no panel behind the characters. This is stated twice on purpose: a row that comes back on a dark or gradient background cannot be cut out and is rejected, and it is the failure that has wasted the most generations.

---8<--- PROMPT ENDS ---8<---


{VIEW} = FRONT ROW
------------------
THE VIEW: all three sprites seen from the FRONT, facing the viewer head-on, shoulders and hips SQUARE to the camera in every frame — both sides of the body equally visible, face pointing straight at the viewer. Never rotated into a side or three-quarter pose; the walk is never shown by turning the body.

HER HEAD MUST READ AS A HEAD. Draw the head as a distinct rounded shape sitting ABOVE the shoulder line with a THICK BLACK OUTLINE between the bottom of the head and the shoulders. If the character has floppy ears, each ear is drawn in a DARKER shade of fur than the head, with a thick black outline separating it from the head behind it. Do not merge head, ears and shoulders into one flat lump of colour with a hairstyle stuck on top.

THE LEGS. In every frame BOTH legs and BOTH feet are fully visible below the torso as two separate vertical columns, with a clear gap of background between them. Never fuse the two legs into one mass, never cross them, never splay them sideways, never raise a thigh.

THE MIDDLE FRAME IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS. Frame 2 (the middle one) = STANDING STILL: both feet flat on the ground at exactly the same height, both legs straight, both arms hanging straight down at the sides. Calm and symmetrical. Draw this one carefully — the cutter builds the walk out of it (build_sheet.py --build-steps), so a clean standing pose with a visible gap between the legs is worth more than any amount of effort on the other two.

Frames 1 and 3 are mid-step: one foot lifted two or three pixels off the ground (heel up, leg still vertical), the other flat and planted, the opposite arm swung forward, body one pixel lower than frame 2. Frame 3 is the opposite step to frame 1. These two are drawn as a fallback — the cutter normally replaces them — so do not sacrifice the middle frame for them.


{VIEW} = SIDE ROW
-----------------
THE VIEW: all three sprites in strict SIDE PROFILE FACING RIGHT — head in profile, nose pointing right, one shoulder to the viewer — in every frame INCLUDING the standing one. Never turned to face the viewer.

Frame 2 (the MIDDLE one) = STANDING STILL: both legs straight and together directly under the body, feet level, arms hanging relaxed, no stride and no lean.

Frame 1 = mid-stride with the LEFT foot planted forward and the right foot back, a clear gap of white between them, the opposite arm swung forward.

Frame 3 = the opposite stride: the RIGHT foot planted forward and the left foot back, arms swapped. Clearly NOT a repeat of the standing pose in frame 2.


{VIEW} = BACK ROW
-----------------
THE VIEW: all three sprites seen from DIRECTLY BEHIND, walking away from the viewer — the back of the head and body, both arms at the sides, shoulders and hips SQUARE to the camera in every frame. NO face, NO eyes, NO snout in any frame. It is a full standing body seen from behind — head, shoulders, torso, legs, visible feet — never a shapeless mass of hair. Never rotated into a side or three-quarter pose.

HER HEAD MUST READ AS A HEAD. Draw the head as a distinct rounded shape sitting ABOVE the shoulder line with a THICK BLACK OUTLINE between the bottom of the head and the shoulders. If the character has floppy ears, each ear is drawn in a DARKER shade of fur than the head, with a thick black outline separating it from the head behind it. Do not merge head, ears and shoulders into one flat lump of colour with a hairstyle stuck on top. This matters most from behind, where there is no face to anchor the head: five back rows in a row came back as one wide lump with a mohawk on it, and darker outlined ears plus a black line at the shoulders is what finally fixed it.

THE HEAD IS A SEPARATE ROUND SHAPE ON TOP OF THE SHOULDERS, NO WIDER THAN HALF THE SHOULDER WIDTH, with empty background on both sides of it. THE HEAD IS NARROWER THAN THE SHOULDERS, with empty background visible on BOTH sides of it and a clear neck between it from the shoulders. Both floppy ears hang down on either side of the head, drawn a shade darker than the head and outlined against it, so the head is a separate shape and not the top of one wide lump. Between the bottom of the head and the shoulders draw a short NECK — a couple of pixels of the jacket's collar, fully outlined — so there is a visible join. If the head, the ears and the shoulders end up as one continuous block of fur-coloured pixels with a mohawk on top, the row is wrong: that exact result has come back seven times.

THE OUTFIT IS THE SAME OUTFIT, SEEN FROM BEHIND. A jacket still covers the torso AND both arms down to the wrists from the back — never drop it to become a skirt, a belt or a bag around the hips, and never leave the torso in bare fur or a plain sweater. Whatever the character wears on its chest in the front row covers its back here, in the same colours, with the same collar, studs and trim.

THE LEGS. In every frame BOTH legs and BOTH feet are fully visible below the torso as two separate vertical columns, with a clear gap of background between them. Never fuse the two legs into one mass, never cross them, never splay them sideways, never raise a thigh.

THE MIDDLE FRAME IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS — same as the front row above. Frame 2 = standing still, both feet flat, legs straight and separated, arms hanging down. Frames 1 and 3 are mid-step fallbacks that the cutter normally replaces.
